nameStory: Corn mint gets its name from its habit of growing as a weed in cornfields and other cultivated areas, where farmers would encounter its strong minty fragrance while working their crops. The name 'field mint' tells the same story - this is the mint you'd stumble upon in agricultural fields rather than carefully tended herb gardens. Unlike its more famous garden cousins, this mint chose the wild, working landscape as its home.
description: Corn mint is a low-growing, spreading perennial herb that reaches 1-2 feet tall with a distinctive square stem that marks it as a member of the mint family. Its small, pale purple or white flowers cluster in dense whorls around the stem at leaf joints, rather than forming the spike-like flower heads of other mints. The oval, toothed leaves release a strong, classic mint fragrance when crushed, though it's often described as earthier and less refined than spearmint or peppermint. This hardy wild mint spreads by underground runners, forming patches in wet, disturbed soils.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small pale purple, pink, or white flowers arranged in dense, ball-like clusters (whorls) around the square stem at each leaf joint, never forming a terminal spike like other mints

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval, serrated leaves arranged in opposite pairs that release a strong, earthy mint fragrance when crushed or brushed against

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low, spreading plant that forms patches through underground runners, typically 1-2 feet tall with a sprawling rather than upright growth pattern

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Distinctly square stems that feel angular when rolled between your fingers, often reddish-tinged and slightly hairy

habitat: Look for corn mint along stream banks, in wet meadows, and around pond edges where the soil stays consistently moist. It thrives in disturbed, muddy areas like ditches, field edges, and the margins of wetlands, often growing alongside sedges, cattails, and other moisture-loving plants. This adaptable mint also pops up in cultivated fields and gardens with rich, damp soil.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges from underground runners with fresh, aromatic leaves that are excellent for identification through their minty fragrance.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with distinctive whorled flower clusters appearing at leaf joints from July through September.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade to small nutlet seeds while leaves may turn yellowish before dying back, though the mint fragrance remains strong.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely above ground, but established patches will reliably return from their underground runner system.

funFact: Corn mint is one of the primary sources of natural menthol used worldwide - in some parts of Asia, entire fields are cultivated just to extract the cooling compound that makes your toothpaste tingle and your throat lozenges feel refreshing.
confusionNotes: Corn mint is easily confused with other wild mints, but remember 'whorls not spires' - its flowers cluster around the stem at leaf joints rather than forming pointed flower spikes at the stem tips like spearmint or peppermint. The earthy, less sweet fragrance is also a good clue.
contextualKnowledge: Botanists sometimes lump corn mint together with Canada mint as varieties of the same species, which explains why you might see conflicting information in different field guides. Both are part of a complex group of closely related wild mints that can be challenging even for experts to distinguish.
compareHints: Unlike spearmint and peppermint which form terminal flower spikes, corn mint's flowers cluster in whorls around the stem at leaf joints. Canada mint is nearly identical but tends to prefer more northern locations and may have slightly different leaf shapes. Corn mint has a more sprawling growth habit than the more upright horse mint and lacks the fuzzy, apple-scented leaves of apple mint.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Canada mint differs from its relatives by having flowers clustered in the leaf joints rather than in terminal spikes like spearmint, and it's strictly a wetland plant while corn mint tolerates drier soils.
Spearmint differs from other New England mints by its nearly hairless leaves and sweet, mild fragrance.
Among New England's mints, apple mint stands out immediately for its fuzzy, rounded leaves that feel like velvet.
Unlike Canada mint which prefers moist but not waterlogged soils, watermint truly loves having wet feet and grows right at the water's edge.
Horse mint differs from our common native Canada mint by being much taller and having woolly-white stems rather than smooth ones.
